extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature—scientists, researchers and clinicians (particularly psychologists, anthropologists, and medical researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the quality of experimental psychological and ethnological research and its application — covering field observation, experimental design (controls, blinding, repeated measures), interpretation, reproducibility, and translation to clinical/industrial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise, methodical field observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should be 'models of precise, methodical observations in the field of ethnological psychology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect comparative data across field sites (e.g., Torres Straits, Egypt, Todas); emphasize detailed, systematic recording in ethnological/psychological fieldwork so that observations can serve as enduring models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insistence on scientific procedure and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain 'insistence on scientific procedure' and a 'delight in scientific analysis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt rigorous scientific habits of mind: explicit procedures, careful analysis, and critical scrutiny of results rather than speculative or anecdotal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of methods to novel experimental conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the 'facility in adapting scientific methods to novel experimental conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify laboratory techniques appropriately for field conditions or unusual subject populations while retaining scientific rigor; innovation in method is valued when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of blinded placebo/control to avoid suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Disguise the drug and prepare a 'control mixture which was indistinguishable from it' so the subject 'never know[s] which he was drinking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement blinding and indistinguishable placebos to control for suggestion, expectation, and sensory/artifactual influences when studying drug or treatment effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for withdrawal and other confounds (washout periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid confounding by prior substance use: 'most of his experiments were carried out more than twelve months after the taking of these drinks had been discontinued.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow adequate washout/adjustment periods and account for withdrawal or long-term effects of prior exposures before testing to prevent misattribution of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repeated measures and baseline comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain several sets of measurements each day (e.g., 'each set consisting usually of six ergograms taken at intervals of two minutes'), with the first set serving as a standard for the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple trials, use within-day baselines and standardized timing/intervals to increase reliability and detect patterns beyond single measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and caution when experiments lack identical replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that 'Head’s experiment has never been identically repeated' and that 'divergent results ... are at least partly due to their employment of different methods of procedure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat unreplicated findings cautiously; encourage identical or closely matched replication before definitive conclusions; note methodological differences when comparing studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical scrutiny and improvement of previous methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to 'previous faulty methods of investigation' and improve on them; Rivers' 'devotion to scientific methods and accuracy' advanced the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate earlier work critically, identify methodological flaws, and design improved procedures to test established claims rather than accepting them uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct physiological effects from indirect sensory or contextual effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret results carefully: an equivalent quantity of whisky gave immediate increase in muscular work—'strongly suggests the influence of sensory stimulation rather than the direct effect of the drug.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing intervention effects, separate pharmacological/physiological mechanisms from indirect influences (e.g., sensory stimulation, suggestion, emotion, novelty). Design controls to parse these alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate psychological phenomena with physiological measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a 'biological standpoint, correlating the psychological with the physiological' and study 'variations in the actions of drugs on different persons' to understand temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate physiological measurements with psychological assessment to explore individual differences and to hypothesize biological bases of behavior or susceptibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate experimental findings to clinical and practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply laboratory training and experimental results to treatment and real problems: Rivers' 'rationale of his successful treatment of the psychoneuroses were directly due to his psychological training' and he applied psychology to 'industrial and commercial work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical insights to inform clinical practice, therapeutic approaches, and industrial/occupational improvements (fatigue study, motion study, vocational selection), ensuring application is evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gain first-hand practical experience relevant to applied work
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain direct experience (e.g., Rivers 'took numerous flights... so that he might gain adequate experience of flying') to better treat patients and test candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where practical application is intended, researchers/clinicians should seek firsthand exposure to the operational context to inform assessment, intervention, and selection procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider context-specific causes rather than one-size-fits-all theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish causes by context: in warfare and occupations like mining the conflicting instincts 'were not sexual, but were the danger instincts,' unlike certain civil-life psychoneuroses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for situational and occupational differences when diagnosing or theorising about disorders; avoid universal causal attributions without context-sensitive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value interdisciplinary breadth and resist excessive specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Warn that 'specialisation has ... reached such a pitch that it has become a serious evil' and that breadth should not be treated with suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cross-disciplinary knowledge and the application of insights across domains; reward researchers who combine wide interests with methodological competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific virtues: thoroughness, accuracy, critical judgement, and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Enduring contributions arise from 'thoroughness and accuracy combined with criticism and genius' together with 'honest, generous character' and devotion to scientific work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both methodological quality (thoroughness, accuracy, critical thought) and personal virtues (integrity, generosity, devotion) as markers of a researcher's reliability and lasting impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to revising theories and acknowledge speculative limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that later speculations (e.g., sudden evolutionary additions of intelligence) may be contested, yet value the 'stimulating, suggestive, and fruitful character' of such work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between well-supported empirical results and broader speculative theorising; present speculative ideas cautiously and welcome critical engagement and revision.
